name: Crabgrass
id_tips: Light-green, wide-bladed grass that sprawls flat in thin spots along drives and walks. Seedlings appear from late April; finger-like seed heads in August; dies at the first frost and leaves bare spots.
when: Prevent at redbud bloom (by April 15). Kill escapes while young (June–July). Overseed the gaps in September.
cultural: Thick, tall turf (4 in tall in summer) shades out seedlings; overseed thin areas every fall; skip spring and summer nitrogen.
control: **Prevent:** dithiopyr (Hi-Yield with Dimension) or prodiamine (LESCO Stonewall, Barricade), watered in. **Late?** Dithiopyr also kills crabgrass up to about 4 weeks after it emerges. **Escapes:** quinclorac (Ortho Weed B-gon + Crabgrass Control, Drive XLR8) or Tenacity plus surfactant on young plants. Mature August crabgrass: let frost kill it.
note: Crabgrass germinates once soil at 1 in holds ~55°F; the first seedlings appear after a week averaging 57–63°F (Fidanza 1996).

name: Yellow nutsedge
id_tips: Shiny, yellow-green, V-shaped leaves in threes on a triangular stem ("sedges have edges"). It grows faster than the lawn, so it pokes up a few days after mowing, and loves wet spots.
when: Late May–June, while plants are young (before 5 leaves).
cultural: Fix drainage and stop overwatering. Pulling it snaps off the tubers (nutlets), which resprout.
control: Halosulfuron (SedgeHammer) or sulfentrazone (Ortho Nutsedge Killer); a second application 6–10 weeks later if needed. Don't mow 2 days before or after SedgeHammer.

name: Dandelion
id_tips: Rosette of jagged leaves, yellow flowers and puffball seed heads; deep taproot.
when: Best: late September–November. Spring spraying during bloom is less effective.
cultural: Thick turf; mulch-mow fall leaves (up to 80% fewer dandelions in a Michigan State study). Dig small numbers with a weeding fork, getting most of the root.
control: Broadleaf herbicide (SpeedZone EW) on a day ≥50°F with no rain for 24 h; spot-spray rather than blanket.

name: White clover
id_tips: Three round leaflets, often with a pale "V"; white ball-shaped flowers; creeping stems that root as they go.
when: Fall (late September–November) if you want it gone.
cultural: Clover fixes its own nitrogen and signals a hungry lawn; a normal fall feeding program thins it. Many people keep some for the bees. Just mow off the flowers before using any insecticide.
control: Triclopyr (Ortho Weed B Gon Chickweed, Clover & Oxalis) or SpeedZone EW in fall.

name: Henbit & purple deadnettle
id_tips: Square stems, scalloped leaves and small purple flowers in March–April. It sprouts in fall and dies by late May.
when: Fall: a pre-emergent on unseeded areas in September, or spray young plants in October–November.
cultural: Thick fall turf prevents it. Spring spraying of flowering henbit is mostly wasted, since it's already dying.
control: SpeedZone EW or triclopyr in fall; K-State suggests a fall pre-emergent where you aren't seeding.

name: Chickweed
id_tips: Low mats of small, pointed, paired leaves and tiny white star flowers in early spring; common in shade and new seedings.
when: Fall, or mild (≥50°F) days in March.
cultural: Improve density; hand-pull mats in beds.
control: Triclopyr (Ortho Chickweed, Clover & Oxalis) or SpeedZone EW.

name: Ground ivy (creeping Charlie)
id_tips: Creeping square stems with round scalloped leaves, a minty smell when mowed, and purple flowers in April. Loves shade and damp spots.
when: Fall is best (October, around the first light frost), then again in spring.
cultural: More light and a thicker lawn; better drainage.
control: Triclopyr products, repeated; hard to kill in one shot.

name: Wild violet
id_tips: Heart-shaped glossy leaves with purple or white flowers in April; the waxy leaves shed herbicide.
cultural: Dig small patches; tolerate them in shady edges (they're native and host fritillary butterflies).
control: Triclopyr in fall, repeated.

name: Nimblewill
id_tips: Wiry, short, blue-green grass in patches. It greens late in spring and turns tan with the first frost.
cultural: Thicken the lawn; it thrives in thin, shaded, wet areas.
control: Mesotrione (Tenacity plus surfactant), 2–3 applications 2–3 weeks apart; or spot-kill with glyphosate in August and reseed.

name: Bermudagrass (wiregrass)
id_tips: Fine, wiry grass that runs by above- and below-ground stems into fescue and beds. Tan from the first frost until May; seed heads look like little bird feet.
when: August, while it's actively growing, then seed in September.
cultural: Edge beds deeply; it creeps in from neighbors and alleys.
control: Spot-spray glyphosate in early August and again about a month later (one spray rarely kills it), then seed 7 days later (MU G6700). In flower beds, fluazifop (Ortho Grass B Gon) kills it without harming broadleaf ornamentals.

name: Zoysia patches
id_tips: Dense, stiff, tan patches in a fescue lawn from October to May that spread slowly outward.
when: August, same as bermudagrass, or learn to live with it.
control: Glyphosate spot-kill in August, a second spray, then reseed.

name: Wild onion & wild garlic
id_tips: Clumps of round leaves (hollow in wild garlic, solid in wild onion) that grow faster than the grass in late winter; strong onion smell.
cultural: Dig clumps, bulbs and all, when the soil is moist.
control: A broadleaf product labeled for wild onion; crush or mow the waxy leaves first so it sticks. It takes repeat applications.

name: Prostrate spurge
id_tips: Flat mats of tiny paired leaves (often with a red spot) and milky sap; thrives in hot, thin, compacted spots and sidewalk cracks.
cultural: Thicken turf; relieve compaction with core aeration.
control: Hand-pull young mats; a broadleaf product labeled for spurge on young plants.

name: Plantain (broadleaf & buckhorn)
id_tips: Broadleaf: wide oval leaves with ribs in a rosette. Buckhorn: narrow ribbed leaves. Both mark compacted soil.
cultural: Core aerate to relieve compaction.
control: SpeedZone EW or a similar 2,4-D product in fall.

name: Yellow woodsorrel (oxalis)
id_tips: Clover-like heart-shaped leaflets, small yellow flowers and seed pods that pop.
when: Late spring–summer on young plants, or fall.
control: Triclopyr (Ortho Chickweed, Clover & Oxalis).

name: Annual bluegrass (Poa annua)
id_tips: Light-green clumps with whitish seed heads in April–May that die in summer heat, leaving holes.
when: Prevent in early September on areas you aren't seeding.
cultural: Overseed in fall to fill the voids it leaves.
control: A fall pre-emergent (prodiamine or dithiopyr) on unseeded areas; no simple homeowner fix once it's up.

name: Brown patch
aka: Rhizoctonia large patch of tall fescue
symptoms: Circular tan patches from 6 in to several feet across; leaves with tan lesions and dark-brown borders; sometimes a grayish "smoke ring" at the patch edge on humid mornings.
when: Nights ≥65°F with dew and humidity (K-State homeowner guide; K-State's commercial guide uses 68°F), usually July–August.
cultural: No spring or summer nitrogen: in K-State plots, spring-fed turf had 48–66% brown patch vs 2–23% for fall-only. Water only in the early morning, mow when dry, and don't overseed at excessive rates. A little bluegrass in the mix helped in New Jersey research.
control: Usually recovers in fall without spraying. For lawns hit hard every year: preventive azoxystrobin (Scotts DiseaseEx) from late June, rotating with propiconazole (BioAdvanced Fungus Control), per label intervals.

name: Gray leaf spot
symptoms: Gray-brown oval leaf spots with dark borders and twisted, dying leaf tips during hot, humid late-summer weather; often worst on young seedlings and ryegrass-heavy stands.
cultural: Avoid ryegrass-heavy mixes, don't push nitrogen in late summer, water only in the morning.
control: Preventive fungicides only where it recurs; ask MU Extension to confirm the diagnosis first.

name: Dollar spot
symptoms: Silver-dollar-size straw-colored spots that merge; hourglass-shaped tan lesions with reddish-brown borders on blades; cobwebby threads on dewy mornings.
cultural: It signals low nitrogen and long leaf wetness. A normal fall feeding program and morning-only watering usually fix it.
control: Fungicide rarely needed on home lawns.

name: Rust
symptoms: Orange dust that rubs off on shoes and the mower; yellowed, thin turf in late summer; worst on slow-growing, under-fed lawns.
cultural: Fall nitrogen speeds growth, so you mow off the infected leaves. Keep mowing regularly.
control: Fungicide rarely needed.

name: Red thread
symptoms: Pink-red threads on leaf tips and tan patches in cool, wet weather.
cultural: Low nitrogen favors it; the fall feeding program usually solves it.
control: Cosmetic; no spray needed.

name: Pythium blight
symptoms: Greasy, dark, water-soaked streaks following drainage paths during very hot, humid, wet spells (nights near 70°F or warmer); white cottony growth on dewy mornings; can kill turf quickly.
cultural: Fix drainage; avoid evening watering and summer nitrogen.
control: Needs a specific fungicide; get a diagnosis from MU Extension.

name: Fairy ring
symptoms: Dark-green rings or arcs, sometimes with mushrooms or a ring of dead grass, fed by decaying organic matter (old stumps, buried wood).
cultural: Mask with regular fall feeding; core aerate and deep-water the ring.
control: No easy cure; it's mostly cosmetic.

name: Slime mold
symptoms: Gray, white or yellow powdery or slimy growth on grass blades after wet weather.
control: Mow or hose it off; it doesn't hurt the grass.

name: White grubs
symptoms: Irregular brown patches in late summer that roll up like carpet because the roots are eaten; skunks, raccoons or birds digging.
threshold: 5–10 grubs per sq ft (MU). Cut 1-sq-ft flaps 2–3 in deep at the edge of damage in 3–4 spots and count.
control: **Prevent** (only if you had damage): chlorantraniliprole (Scotts GrubEx1) in May, or imidacloprid May–June, watered in. **Cure** active damage (late July–September): trichlorfon (BioAdvanced 24 Hour Grub Killer Plus), watered in with ½ in within 24 hours.
note: Grub control won't get rid of moles; they mostly eat earthworms.

name: Sod webworm
symptoms: Small ragged brown spots, chewed blades, green pellet droppings; buff moths zig-zag over the lawn at dusk.
threshold: Soap flush: pour 2 Tbsp dish soap in 1 gallon of water over 1 sq yd; treat only if many caterpillars come up (roughly 15 or more).
control: Bt for young larvae; a lawn insecticide labeled for sod webworms for heavy infestations. Healthy fescue usually outgrows the damage.

name: Fall armyworm
symptoms: Patches brown out almost overnight in late summer and fall, especially new seedings; green-to-brown striped caterpillars with an inverted "Y" on the head.
threshold: Soap flush; roughly 3 or more per sq ft.
control: A lawn insecticide labeled for armyworms, applied in the evening. Established fescue usually regrows; new seedings may need reseeding.

name: Cicada killer wasps
symptoms: Huge wasps digging holes with dirt piles in bare, sunny spots in July–August. Males buzz you but can't sting; females rarely sting.
control: Tolerate them (they're gone by September). Thicken or mulch bare spots to discourage nesting.

name: Moles
symptoms: Raised tunnels and volcano-shaped mounds, most active in moist spring and fall soil.
control: Trapping is the only reliable method (scissor or harpoon trap on an active runway). Grub control doesn't work; moles mostly eat earthworms. Repellents and home remedies are unreliable.

name: Voles
symptoms: Surface runways (2-in-wide paths) in the grass after snow melts; gnawed bark at the base of shrubs and young trees.
control: Lawn damage is usually cosmetic: rake it and it fills in. Protect trunks with hardware cloth; snap traps with peanut butter under a cover.

name: Rabbits
symptoms: Beans, lettuce and tulips chewed to the ground; clean 45° cuts on twigs; girdled young trunks in winter.
control: A 2-ft fence of 1-in mesh (bottom buried 3–6 in) around the garden; hardware-cloth trunk guards in November; repellents need regular reapplying.

name: Dog urine spots
symptoms: Round dead spots ringed by dark-green grass.
control: Soak the spot with water soon after; reseed dead patches in September.

name: Dull mower blade or scalping
symptoms: Tan, frayed leaf tips a day after mowing (dull blade), or yellow-brown stripes over bumps (scalping).
control: Sharpen the blade (about every 25 hours of mowing) and raise the deck.

name: Drought dormancy (brown summer lawn)
symptoms: Straw-colored lawn after weeks of heat and little rain, often starting on slopes and near pavement.
control: Tug test: dormant grass holds firm with white, firm crowns; dead grass pulls out. Keep traffic off; after ~3 weeks without ½ in of rain in the heat, give ½–1 in every 2–3 weeks to keep crowns alive. It greens up 1–2 weeks after soaking fall rains.
